stories.headline: Houthis threaten Saudi Aramco facilities as government forces advance in Yemen
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Yemen’s Houthi group warned civilians and employees to evacuate Saudi Arabia’s Aramco oil facilities on Tuesday, calling them “a legitimate target,” after the Saudi-led coalition ordered an evacuation near a Yemeni oil station in the Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said any strikes on Sanaa would be met with a “harsh and painful” response in Riyadh. Shortly after the coalition’s evacuation order, explosions were reported in Sanaa; Houthi-affiliated media said Saudi-backed air strikes hit an oil facility in the al-Sabaha area. Al Jazeera correspondent Yousef Mawry reported that Saudi Arabia also struck oil storage tanks at Ras Isa port and an oil station in Hodeidah province.

The Houthi threats follow a weekend of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia. At least 14 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in separate Houthi missile strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport, according to multiple sources. Another person was killed and 11 wounded on Sunday after a projectile struck the airport. Several international airlines, including Air France-KLM, Air India, Etihad, Lufthansa, Delta, Gulf Air and Qatar Airways, suspended flights to Saudi Arabia and neighboring countries. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted three drones north of Riyadh on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia’s cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Houthis would face “consequences” for the attacks, according to the Saudi Press Agency.

On the ground in Yemen, government forces advanced as part of operation “Dawn of Yemen,” a counteroffensive launched just over a week ago after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast in September, including the port city of Mocha and areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait. Military spokesman Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili said operations had involved 1,879 precise strikes, neutralizing 950 Houthi fighters and destroying 380 military vehicles. Government troops captured strategic heights around the Maas camp in Marib’s Medghal district and positions north of the Harib district. In Taiz governorate, government forces conducted nine air strikes and reported capturing 81 Houthi fighters in al-Dhabab. Fierce clashes continued across multiple axes in Taiz, where the Houthis have the city under siege.

The escalation has caused heavy civilian casualties. The Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedom said the Houthis killed at least five civilians, including a five-year-old girl, and wounded 17 others in Taiz over 24 hours, firing more than 180 projectiles at residential areas. A Houthi attack struck al-Safwa Hospital, shattering windows and injuring at least one person. Yemen’s Ministry of Public Health said medicines and fuel at Taiz health facilities were “nearing depletion.” The International Committee of the Red Cross warned that civilians across the Middle East are paying an “unacceptable price.” At least 46 civilians have been killed in Yemen since August, and more than 200,000 people have been displaced since September, according to the United Nations and its migration agency.

The conflict, which began in 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa, has drawn in a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government since 2015. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely held until renewed escalation in 2026. Analysts describe Saudi Arabia as facing an asymmetric struggle: the Houthis can impose high costs without defeating Saudi forces, and Riyadh must weigh its military options against economic security and regional alliances. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that Iran must engage in serious negotiations, accusing Tehran of destabilizing the region. Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty urged his Iranian counterpart to halt Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, though analysts say Iran holds limited sway over the group. The Houthis have also threatened a “swift and painful” response if the United States intervenes.

stories.headline: Indian opposition leaders arrested as protests over voter rolls intensify
body: Leaders of India's Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) were detained early Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site in New Delhi, as demonstrations demanding the resignation of the country's chief election commissioner over a controversial revision of electoral rolls continued to escalate. Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing CJP co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory long used for protests. Footage showed the two, along with others, climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag. The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar would no longer be a designated protest venue, instead identifying three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.

The protests, led by the CJP and joined by opposition parties, are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar after more than 130 million names were reportedly removed from electoral rolls nationwide. Critics say the voter list revision is politically motivated and risks disenfranchising eligible voters, alleging it benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The BJP and the Election Commission deny the allegations, saying the move is needed to clean up the rolls. Anger over the revision intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration; the Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.

Over the weekend, authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital, deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel, closing several metro stations, and disrupting train services. According to local media, at least 3,000 people were detained across the city. Police also detained CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke from the plane in which he landed in New Delhi on Saturday. Videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses. On Monday, opposition parties held a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court, and the Congress party, India's main opposition party, petitioned the court challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise.

The CJP began as a satirical online movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant referred to unemployed young people as 'cockroaches' during a court hearing in May. The group led weeks of protests earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms, which culminated in the resignation of the federal education minister. Analysts say the government's response this time — including mass security deployments, preemptive detentions, and the removal of Jantar Mantar as a protest site — reflects lessons learned from the earlier protests. However, experts note that the current protests, focused on voter rolls, have not matched the cross-cutting appeal of the education issue, and they consider an abrupt change of government unlikely given India's strong state institutions.

stories.headline: South Korean stocks plunge 5.5%, stoking global chip fears
body: South Korean stocks plunged on Tuesday, with the KOSPI benchmark falling 5.5% to its lowest level in about three months and deepening a global selloff in chip stocks. The index now sits roughly 38% below its June all-time high. Chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics, which together account for more than half of the South Korean market's capitalization, fell 10% and 7%, respectively.

The selloff was fueled by mounting worries over the artificial-intelligence trade. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned that speculative AI investing resembles gambling in a casino, according to the Financial Times, intensifying questions about whether infrastructure spending will generate sufficient returns. Investors are now looking to Thursday's earnings from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., widely viewed as the next major test of the AI investment thesis. stories.headline: Chip stocks slump as AI investment doubts deepen
body: Shares of semiconductor companies fell sharply on Tuesday, driven by a combination of AI investment skepticism and new competitive pressure from China. The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped more than 100 points, or 0.35%, in early trading, while Asian markets saw steeper declines: South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled 6.25%, Japan’s Nikkei fell 1.8%, and the Taiwan exchange lost nearly 2%. Major chip stocks including Samsung Electronics (down 7.4%), SK Hynix (down 10%), Tokyo Electron (down 7.15%), and TSMC (down about 2%) all retreated. On Wall Street, Micron Technology slid 4.8%, Advanced Micro Devices dropped 1.4%, Nvidia lost 0.8%, and Broadcom slipped 0.2%.

The sell-off was fueled by two developments. First, Broadcom CEO Hock Tan likened many AI investors to casino gamblers, saying at a conference in Singapore that “a lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in” and that they “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino.” Tan noted that AI companies such as OpenAI remain lossmaking despite $50 billion in annualized revenue at the end of September, adding that “it doesn’t tell anything at this point except that there is a lot of potential revenue growth.” He also warned that a sizeable portion of AI labs’ enterprise revenue comes from pilot projects, comparing it to a child spending tokens at a video arcade without learning anything.

Second, Chinese memory chip maker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) announced progress on a new “4F square” stacked DRAM architecture that promises to increase storage density. CXMT, which debuted on the Shanghai stock market in late July with a $487 billion market capitalization, plans to begin producing high-bandwidth memory (HBM) later this year. Investors fear the company could challenge dominant memory chip makers Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. “The rout in chip stocks seems set to continue thanks once again to news from China,” said Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG. “CXMT’s new developments remind investors of the huge competition in the sector.”

The broader market showed mixed results. The Dow Jones industrial average rose nearly 0.4% in early trading, while the FTSE 100 in London hit a three-week high, gaining 0.73% to 10,762, supported by gains in financial stocks, retreating oil prices, and easing bond yields. Brent crude dropped 1.2% to $105.36 a barrel. AI shares have been volatile in recent months amid concerns that companies are spending heavily on AI infrastructure funded by debt.

Sandisk stock fell an additional 3.5% on Tuesday after shedding 6% on Monday, as CXMT’s advances renewed fears of competition in memory chips. However, analysts noted that CXMT’s chips primarily target the low-end mobile phone market rather than AI data centers, and CXMT is not yet producing NAND chips, which are Sandisk’s specialty. “I see greater risk to Micron stock than to Sandisk,” one analyst wrote. The broader concern remains that Chinese competition could pressure margins across the sector, even as memory supply remains in deficit and may tighten further next year.

stories.headline: Visa receives Beijing approval to set up bank card clearing business in China
body: Visa announced Tuesday that it had received approval from the People's Bank of China (PBOC) to set up a bank card clearing business in the country, opening the door for the U.S. payments giant to serve mainland China's domestic payments market for the first time. "This marks an important milestone toward the company serving China's domestic payments market," Visa said in a statement.

Visa CEO Ryan McInerney said: "For more than 40 years, Visa has been an active contributor to China's dynamic payments landscape. We look forward to taking the necessary steps in the process, pursuant to the PBOC's regulations, to begin operating domestically in China." Visa previously said it applied with the PBOC in May 2020 to operate a bank card clearing institution.

The approval arrives as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping plan their third meeting this year. McInerney joined Trump's business delegation to Beijing in May and became chair of the U.S.-China Business Council in June; he also led a trip to Beijing in early September. Trump told Fox News after his Beijing trip that he raised Visa's request for China market access, and after the September summit China said it would approve applications from all foreign financial institutions to operate in the country.

"The timing is notable," said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group. "Beijing chose to approve Visa's license just ahead of the APEC Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen next month, where Xi and Trump are expected to meet again. The move suggests that Beijing is keen to demonstrate tangible progress for American businesses before Trump's next visit to China."

Mainland China has historically maintained tight control over its financial sector, favoring domestic players and restricting cross-border capital flows. Visa has worked with Chinese banks on dual-branded cards, for which China's UnionPay processes transactions domestically and Visa handles payments overseas; in January, Visa said mainland China-issued cards could be linked to Apple Pay for use overseas. Rivals have already entered the market: Mastercard's joint venture began processing payments in 2024 after receiving PBOC approval for clearing preparations in February 2020, while American Express was the first, obtaining its processing license in June 2020 after a PBOC nod in 2018.

Mobile payments dominate daily consumer transactions in China, led by Tencent's WeChat and Alibaba-affiliate Ant's Alipay. Visa said it would take the necessary steps under PBOC regulations to begin operating domestically in the country.

stories.headline: Football regulator vows to quit over political interference in Man City case
body: David Kogan, chairman of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR), has said he would resign if political interference compromised any potential investigation into Manchester City, which is appealing a guilty verdict for breaching Premier League financial rules. Speaking at the launch of the regulator's 'State of the Game' report in Manchester on Tuesday, Kogan said his independence and the regulator's were absolute, and that no politician had attempted to influence the body. Asked directly whether he would quit if pressured, Kogan replied: "I would resign."

The case stems from an independent commission's finding that Manchester City broke Premier League rules between 2009 and 2018 by creating "sham" contracts with commercial partners to secretly channel more than £830m into the club. City deny the allegations and have appealed. If the verdict is upheld, the IFR, which has the power to assess the suitability of club owners and executives, could decide whether to force a sale. Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised last month for saying he would be "really concerned" if City's Abu Dhabi owners departed; he later denied downplaying the seriousness of the findings. Kogan said the regulator is "governed by statute" and that "no comment by any politician or indeed any individual is going to affect what we do."

The independent panel will hold a sanctions hearing that could take months, with possible punishments ranging from a fine, points deduction or ejection from the Premier League to stripping City of eight trophies won during the affected period. City can appeal both the guilty verdicts and any sanction. The commission's report also stated that "a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence." Kogan said the case was "raising very serious issues" and that the regulator would examine whether owners, directors and senior executives are running the club "with probity."

The regulator's independence has been a subject of political scrutiny. A provision in an earlier draft of the Football Governance Bill that would have required the regulator to consider the UK government's trade and foreign policy priorities when assessing owners was removed. Kogan also faced scrutiny over his Labour Party ties after the Commissioner for Public Appointments found that Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy breached rules by failing to register donations from Kogan. Shadow Culture Minister Louie French called him a "Labour donor and key crony," a claim Kogan dismissed, saying his probity "stands up to scrutiny."

The 'State of the Game' report revealed that Premier League spending on legal disputes surged from £45m in 2015-16 to £212m in 2024-25, driven largely by the case against Manchester City and separate challenges to associated party transaction rules. Kogan said any future IFR legal action would ultimately be funded by clubs through the levy mechanism, with the government initially cash-flowing the costs, adding: "We wouldn't go into legal action unless we thought we were going to win."

stories.headline: Rwanda chosen to host African Grand Prix in landmark F1 deal
body: Formula 1 has signed a 10-year deal for Rwanda to host an African Grand Prix from the early 2030s, ending a nearly 40-year absence of the sport from the continent. F1 president Stefano Domenicali hailed the agreement as a "landmark" achievement, announced in Kigali alongside Rwandan President Paul Kagame and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem. The last grand prix in Africa was held in South Africa in 1993.

The race will be held at a new circuit being built in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, as part of a wider development near a new international airport that also includes entertainment, residential, hotels, spas, sports science and an innovation hub. The track, designed by former F1 driver Alex Wurz, is envisaged to be about 6km (3.7 miles) long with 17 corners and nearly 200m of elevation change, using the undulating Rwandan landscape. It is not completely finalised, with further consultation with teams and drivers planned, but the renders released bear similarities to the first part of Suzuka, and Wurz has aimed for a style like Spa-Francorchamps, Suzuka and Mugello.

The deal marks the end of nearly 10 years of effort by F1's owners Liberty Media, which has had an ambition to hold a race in Africa since buying the sport at the start of 2017. Rwanda succeeded where Morocco and South Africa, among others, failed: Morocco never found the finances, and South Africa had up to four separate projects with different promoters in three locations, two in Cape Town. For F1, with other countries interested in slots on an already crowded schedule, that was too much to deal with. The Bugesera site is currently a greenfield site, but insiders say there should be no difficulties completing the project by 2030.

President Kagame backed the project as a way of showcasing his country on the global stage, saying it would bring "jobs, skills, tourism and new business" to Africa. He said he wanted to "pave the way for other races to be hosted on the continent" and that projects such as this act as a catalyst to "help break the cycle" of African athletes achieving on the world stage but the continent getting little in return. "We are not just looking at Rwanda alone," he said. "We are looking at Rwanda in the context of a continent and we have ambitions to bring in our African brothers and sisters to participate." Domenicali said F1 was "showing the world what it means to be a country that has a vision", adding: "Rwanda is one of the world's great success stories... a nation filled with ambition, creativity and determination."

The choice is controversial. Rwanda has previously been accused of sportswashing, and is the subject of a case brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture. Rwanda is fighting off allegations that the project uses money better directed elsewhere in a country that receives international aid, emphasising that funding comes from a newly established development fund combining public and private investment. Last month, it launched a five-year plan aiming to attract £3.5bn in private investment. F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally", and a statement in the context of the announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."

Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns, Felix Jakens, criticised the deal, saying: "Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record. Formula 1 says sport can be 'a positive force for good'. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Formula 1 must not be a bystander. It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise." The F1 calendar already includes countries that have faced similar accusations, including Saudi Arabia, which will host the Fifa World Cup in 2034; boxing has become heavily reliant on Saudi finance. Lewis Hamilton has been pushing the importance of having a grand prix in Africa for some time, and the sport's bosses already recognised the project's importance.

stories.headline: BioNTech mRNA cancer vaccine misses progression-free survival endpoint in Phase 2/3 trial
body: BioNTech’s mRNA cancer immunotherapy BNT113 failed to improve progression-free survival (PFS) compared with Keytruda alone in a Phase 2/3 trial for patients with HPV16-positive head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), the German biotech announced Tuesday. The study, called Ahead-Merit, missed one of its dual primary endpoints, but overall survival (OS) data remain immature, and the independent data monitoring committee recommended the trial continue as planned to evaluate OS, which is the other primary endpoint.

The open-label trial assessed BNT113 in combination with Merck’s checkpoint inhibitor Keytruda versus Keytruda monotherapy. BioNTech reported that PFS was statistically no better on the combination regimen, causing the study to miss that endpoint. However, the statistical design allows a positive trial outcome if OS is eventually shown to be improved. BioNTech’s stock fell 5% to $91.32 in premarket trading from Monday’s close of $95.84, while Moderna’s shares also dipped 3%.

BioNTech Chief Medical Officer Özlem Türeci, M.D., said in a statement that the data show BNT113 “is engaging its intended therapeutic mechanism.” She noted that immune-mediated antitumor effects can build and deepen over time, potentially leading to durable benefits that could be captured in the OS analysis. BNT113 is designed to trigger immune responses against HPV16 oncoproteins E6 and E7 and boost pre-existing T-cell immunity, complementing the T-cell responses induced by Keytruda.

BMO Capital Markets analysts said in a note that it is plausible the immune response takes time to fully deepen, leaving the door open to OS improvement. However, they added that the PFS miss made them “significantly” less confident that BNT113 will extend OS. Precedents exist for cancer immunotherapies improving OS after failing to extend PFS; a Phase 3 trial of Keytruda in HNSCC missed its PFS endpoint but later showed an OS advantage that persisted across five years of follow-up. Still, many trials that miss PFS endpoints subsequently fail on OS.

The results come after hopes for mRNA cancer immunotherapies were lifted in August when Merck & Co. and Moderna reported positive Phase 3 data for their personalized candidate, intismeran autogene. Unlike BNT113, which encodes a fixed set of antigens, intismeran autogene contains antigens tailored to each patient’s tumor mutations. stories.headline: Scientists create first 3D map of brain lipids, revealing 539 distinct regions
body: Researchers at Ecole Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL) have created the first detailed 3D map of lipids in the brain, identifying 539 chemically distinct territories, named 'lipizones,' in a study published in Nature. The Lipid Brain Atlas, built from approximately 7 million measurements across mouse brains, reveals patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed, including surprising complexity within white matter.

Lipids are fatty molecules that form the membranes around neurons, contribute to the myelin insulation of nerve fibers, and play key roles in communication between brain cells. But conventional imaging techniques cannot easily distinguish individual lipid molecules, leaving what Giovanni D'Angelo, professor at the Kristian Gerhard Jebsen Foundation Chair in Nutrition and Metabolism at EPFL, called 'a blurry picture of how lipids differ from one part of the brain to another.' He noted that this gap matters because changes in brain lipids are increasingly linked to conditions from depression to Alzheimer's disease.

To construct the atlas, the team, led by D'Angelo, Luca Fusar Bassini, and Gioele La Manno, used mass spectrometry imaging to scan thin sections of brain tissue. They analyzed 172 different lipids in 109 brain slices from 11 mice, then combined the data into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction using machine learning tools developed for the project. The resulting 539 lipizones each have a characteristic lipid combination, creating a recognizable chemical signature. Some correspond to established brain structures, while others expose chemical boundaries that previous approaches overlooked. 'In effect, lipids work like postal codes, giving distant but related parts of the brain the same chemical address,' D'Angelo said.

The atlas also challenged assumptions about brain uniformity. White matter, the tissue containing nerve fibers that connect brain regions, was found to contain numerous distinct lipid zones rather than a largely consistent composition. 'This shows that the cells which make myelin are far more varied in their chemistry than their genes alone would suggest,' said Fusar Bassini. The researchers also detected previously unrecognized chemical boundaries in the choroid plexus, which produces cerebrospinal fluid, and in the tissues lining the brain's internal cavities.

Examining pregnant mice revealed substantial shifts in lipid composition across numerous brain regions, more pronounced than typical differences between male and female mice. The cortex showed particularly extensive changes, while levels of galactosyl ceramide, an important myelin component, increased sharply throughout much of the brain's white matter. 'Together, these shifts suggest the brain retunes its own wiring to meet the demands of pregnancy,' said La Manno. 'The Atlas reveals that the brain constantly adjusts its lipids to meet the body's changing needs.'

The Lipid Brain Atlas is freely available online, allowing scientists to combine lipid data with existing genetic and cellular maps for a more complete picture of brain organization. It also establishes a reference for healthy mouse brain tissue, which could help investigate how lipid disruptions contribute to development, aging, and disorders such as Alzheimer's and depression. Although the specific mouse map cannot be directly applied to humans, the approach can be used to uncover comparable patterns in the human brain. 'What transfers to humans isn't the map, it's the method, and the fact that we now know that a healthy brain has a very organized lipid map at all,' said Fusar Bassini.

stories.headline: Lancet commission identifies gravest health threats facing humanity; two have 'extinction potential'
body: Dozens of scientific experts, co-chaired by physician and health economist Christopher JL Murray of the University of Washington, have published a sweeping international assessment in The Lancet cataloging 17 major global health threats facing humanity this century. Two were singled out as carrying 'extinction potential' between now and 2100 despite their ultimately low probability: malicious AI — including using AI to create new bioweapons — and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine. The review's key message, its authors said, is that these dangers can be mitigated and managed, but only if society takes action now.

To quantify the stakes, the researchers used modeling to estimate how much death and disability could potentially be avoided for each threat between 2025 and 2100, measured in disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) — where one DALY equals one lost year of healthy life due to premature death or living with illness, injury, or disability. Under the researchers' baseline forecast, the total global burden of disease and injury over that period amounts to an estimated 246 billion DALYs, equivalent to roughly 500 COVID-19 pandemics. Other potentially extinction-level dangers, such as asteroid strikes or supervolcano eruptions, were discounted because their probability of occurring this century is very low, while the hypothetical creation of 'mirror life' was excluded because it has not yet been developed and is too early to quantify.

Beyond the two extinction-level cases, the researchers identified 15 major catastrophic risks, each associated with more than 1 billion potentially avoidable DALYs between now and 2100 — a figure the researchers note is equivalent to two COVID-19 pandemics, 'showing that these are critical threats for governments and the global community to address.' The list comprises air pollution, antimicrobial resistance, childhood malnutrition, climate change, the collapse of international aid funding for health, conventional armed conflict, high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment, naturally occurring pandemics, obesity, poor mental health, smoking, and unhealthy aging.

The largest potentially avoidable burden came from obesity (including the health effects of high BMI, poor diet, and low physical activity), with an estimated 23.1 billion DALYs — corresponding to about 46 COVID-19 pandemics — being the difference between best- and worst-case scenarios by 2100. Low educational attainment and income inequality followed, with higher rates of education projected to reduce the burden of disease both by improving people's health and slowing population growth. The researchers cautioned that because each threat's burden was calculated individually, the totals cannot be added together without over-counting the overlap in health problems individuals face, and they emphasized how interconnected many of these dangers are.

Murray noted that some threats already impose substantial health burdens today, while others carry a real danger if they materialize. 'The striking finding is not only the scale of these threats, but that humanity still has the agency to act,' he said. 'Across all 17 catastrophic threats, the decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and well-being of the next generation.' The commission makes three key recommendations: build and fund threat-ready health systems; dramatically increase investment in breakthrough innovation in areas like health, climate, and technology; and create a 'Monitor of 21st Century Global Threats to Health' to continually track and update threat assessments. Writing in an accompanying editorial, The Lancet's editors said the commission can catalyze international, regional, and national action: 'The unpleasant reality is that the threats we face are multiple, complex, and difficult… Doing so will require all of us to think much more broadly about where the biggest threats lie.'

stories.headline: Google releases Gemini 4 Argon, its long-awaited frontier AI model
body: Google has finally released Gemini 4 Argon, its long-awaited frontier AI model, after months of trailing its rivals in the AI race. The company says Argon can compete with the best the industry has to offer, and it begins rolling out today to higher-tier Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and in AI mode in Search, as well as to Ultra subscribers on Google's agentic development platform Antigravity. It is not clear when — or if — Argon will be available to Plus subscribers or free users.

Google says Argon delivers "frontier reasoning and improved performance across complex workflows" while cutting down on the hedging, repetition, and cliches that continue to plague AI chatbots. The company claims the model outperforms rival models such as OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5.5 across a range of benchmarks, including coding, cybersecurity, science, finance, and law. Google is already putting Argon to use internally, such as finding and patching cybersecurity vulnerabilities, halving the computing power needed to power YouTube's comments section, and debugging the drone physics simulator for Alphabet's drone delivery company Wing.

Argon is being priced very competitively. The model launches with an introductory price of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, around a fifth the cost of OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Fable 5 models. Even after those costs double at the end of November, when the introductory period finishes, Argon will still be significantly cheaper than its frontier rivals on a per-token basis — though this doesn't necessarily translate to lower costs in practice, as models can use different numbers of tokens for the same tasks.

The launch is Argon's first major frontier release since Gemini 3 in late 2025, and fills in some of the blanks left behind when Google first teased the model a few weeks ago. In the intervening months, impressive models from Anthropic and OpenAI have seen Google trail far behind its rivals, while seismic internal shakeups raised further doubts about the company's ability — or desire — to reclaim its position at the frontier of AI. In line with other recent frontier model releases, the public rollout follows a limited release to a select set of "trusted cyber defenders" to be tested for potential risks.

Alongside the release, Google detailed Argon's robotics capabilities in a blog post, calling the model a step change in physical understanding, code generation, and visual-semantic reasoning. Argon scores 87% on the Embodied Reasoning (ERQA) benchmark, which tests a model's ability to understand and solve physical, spatial problems in 3D environments, outperforming every other frontier model. Google says Argon can be applied across the entire robotics lifecycle — robot control, real-to-sim reconstruction, physical understanding, and research and self-improvement — with demonstrations including a Boston Dynamics Spot quadruped learning to dispose of soda cans in a foot-pedal trash bin after practicing on a MuJoCo digital twin, a robotic arm reorienting a fallen mug and putting a crumpled napkin inside it, steering a video world model to rearrange Scrabble tiles to spell A-R-G-O-N, and reconstructing physically calibrated simulation twins from real robot teleoperation footage.

Argon's arrival suggests Google can't be counted out of the AI race just yet. Landing just a day after Meta announced its own frontier model, Muse Wonder Full, Argon is a reminder of how quickly the balance of power can shift in AI, and that the frontier is far from a two-horse race.

stories.headline: Apple Launches HomeView Smart Display, Entering Smart Home Hub Market
body: Apple on Tuesday announced the HomeView, its first smart home display, priced at $299 and available for preorder starting today, with shipping beginning November 13. The device features a 7-inch square Liquid Retina touchscreen, built-in Siri AI, and comes in two models at the same price: a countertop version with a speaker base and a wall-mounted version. However, the wall-mounted model requires a separate mount, starting at $59.95, which is not included in the $299 price.

The HomeView is designed as a smart home controller, personal assistant, and home hub. It can control smart home devices via the Apple Home app, display live feeds from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and authenticate actions like unlocking a door using Face ID or an iPhone. The device runs on Siri AI and, when connected to an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad, can pull personal context from messages, calendar appointments, and emails to take actions, such as setting a coffee maker to turn on based on a contact's arrival time.

The display supports swipe gestures to navigate between customizable "faces" resembling Apple Watch faces, widgets, and on-board apps including Calendar, Messages, Photos, FaceTime, Notes, Reminders, Music, and Podcasts. It also features a guided cooking experience that can transfer recipes from an iPhone via Handoff and reformat them with in-line timers. Other capabilities include FaceTime calls with Center Stage, music playback, and a 12 MP camera that can function as a mirror.

The HomeView can recognize up to six individual household members, automatically showing personalized information such as messages, contacts, and calendar appointments when a person approaches. The wall-mounted version is available in two colors and requires a power solution; Apple offers three mounts from Schneider Home: a Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector starting at $59.95, a Power Mount AC Wired starting at $79.95, and a Power Mount PoE Wired available in early 2027 for $129.95. The countertop model includes a speaker base with a custom down-firing woofer and two passive radiators.

The launch positions Apple in direct competition with Amazon's Echo Show and Google's Nest Hub smart displays. The HomeView is part of a broader push into the home, alongside the announcement of new Apple TV 4K with built-in microphones for Siri, and a new Apple Home Collection including a video doorbell, smart lock, and security cameras. Apple has had a mixed history in the smart home space, with products like the HomePod struggling to match the popularity of competing devices.

stories.headline: Character.AI files for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, agrees to sell some assets to Disney for $20M
stories.byline: Tech / AI desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Character.AI, the five-year-old platform that lets users create and chat with AI characters, has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and agreed to sell some of its assets to Disney for $20 million in a court-supervised sale process. In a court document, the company said it had assets and liabilities of between $50 million and $100 million.

The $20 million deal covers some of Character.AI's assets and a non-exclusive perpetual license for its technology, with Disney providing transition services via former Character.AI employees who joined the entertainment giant last month alongside former CEO Karandeep Singh Anand. "Over the past year, Character.ai has taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve its business in the face of significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds," CEO Colin Adams said in a statement. "After a comprehensive review of the available alternatives, the board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides the Company with the best opportunity to maximize value for all stakeholders."

Adams said the company would continue operating during the sale process, which is expected to close in late November or early December, but noted that no bid for the company's assets or a buyer has yet emerged. "We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down," he wrote.

Founded in late 2021 by former Google engineers Noam Shazeer, a co-author of the landmark Transformer paper, and Daniel De Freitas, Character.AI initially focused on training foundation models and developing a platform for custom AI characters. The startup reached unicorn status in September 2022 with a $150 million fundraise, saying users had exchanged more than 2 billion messages with its bots in five months and averaged more than two hours on the platform daily. Its apps drew more than 1.7 million installs in their first week in May 2023. In August 2024, Google struck a $2.7 billion deal to license the startup's models, and both co-founders returned to the search giant; general counsel Dominic Perella stepped in as interim CEO as the company shifted away from training foundation models to focus on growth. By October 2024, the platform had 20 million monthly active users.

The company's fortunes turned after it was sued following the suicide of a 14-year-old Florida boy whose mother said he became obsessed with a chatbot on the platform, and after Texas launched an investigation into whether the platform complied with child privacy and safety laws. Character.AI subsequently settled some of the lawsuits, added more safety features, and banned minors from its platform. In June of last year, the company appointed Anand, a former Brex and Meta executive, as CEO and expanded into AI video generation and social feeds, later introducing interactive storytelling formats and microdramas. The bankruptcy filing shows those changes could not move the needle on sustainability.

The filing also underscores how difficult it is to scale and monetize consumer-facing AI products. Character.AI was one of the top apps in terms of time spent, according to analytics firm Sensor Tower, but high engagement is a double-edged sword: AI costs rise the more people use the app, increasing the pressure to monetize users. The startup raised more than $193 million in funding from investors including Lightspeed, SV Angel, Greycroft, and a16z, according to PitchBook.

stories.headline: Anthropic's Claude AI submitted false murder tip to Philadelphia police
body: Anthropic's Claude AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia Police Department, the company and police department confirmed on Friday. The false tip was sent on July 18 through the department's website for submitting information about unsolved murders, but it was flagged by a spam filter and never reviewed by a person. Anthropic said it discovered the incident on September 28 and informed the police department on October 8.

The submission occurred during internal testing of Claude Haiku 4.5, according to an Anthropic report describing "unintended model actions we've observed during evaluations and internal use of Claude." The model was instructed to complete various forms up to the final submission stage and to stop before submitting. "Several times Claude mistakenly submitted the form instead, expecting there to be an additional confirmation page," Anthropic said.

In one run, the model landed on a page referencing an unsolved homicide that contained a tip form run by a police department. Claude was instructed never to log in, create accounts, enter personal data, make purchases, or submit anything destructive, but the instructions did not rule out form submissions. Claude filled out the form with the message: "I may have information regarding this case. I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area around [the street named on the page] during that time period. Please contact me if this information is relevant." The false tip left the name and contact fields empty.

Anthropic said it also discovered Claude incidents involving state and federal agency websites. One such incident reportedly involved Claude submitting 20 visa applications to the US State Department. The Philadelphia Police Department issued a lengthy statement on the incident to the ABC station in Philadelphia. The department said the email message generated when the tip was submitted ended up in a spam folder, meaning no person reviewed the false tip.
The Philadelphia Police Department called the two-month delay between the incident and notification "unacceptable," according to the statement.
